questions.question_text: Write $c^{6}\times c^{3}$ as a single power.

options.why: Multiplied the indices ($6\times3$); indices are multiplied for a power of a power, not for a product.
Divided the indices ($6\div3$) instead of adding them.
Wrote the two indices side by side instead of adding them.
Added the indices; the fraction bar means division, so the indices subtract.
Multiplied the indices ($12\times5$) instead of subtracting them.
Put the base underneath even though the numerator has the higher power.

questions.question_text: Simplify $\frac{n^{4}}{n^{11}}$, giving your answer in the form $\frac{1}{\text{base}^{n}}$.

options.why: Found the difference of the indices but left the base on top, though the denominator has the higher power.
Added the indices instead of taking their difference.
Kept the denominator's index without subtracting the numerator's index from it.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{n^{4}}{n^{11}}$
The denominator has the higher power, so the base stays underneath.
$=\frac{1}{n^{11-4}}$
$=\frac{1}{n^{7}}$

options.why: Added the indices; indices are added for a product, but multiplied for a power of a power.
Wrote the two indices side by side instead of multiplying them.
Multiplied the indices correctly but also wrote the outer index in front as a coefficient.

questions.question_text: Which of these expressions **cannot** be written as a single power of one pronumeral using an index law?

options.why: Thought two different indices block the law; the bases match, so the indices add to give $a^{10}$.
Thought a bracketed power is a different base; it is one base, so the indices multiply to give $a^{24}$.
Thought a fraction is not covered by an index law; the bar means division, so the indices subtract to give $a^{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
$a^{4}\times b^{6}$
The bases $a$ and $b$ are different, so no index law applies and the product stays as $a^{4}b^{6}$.

questions.question_text: For which expression do you **multiply** the indices in order to simplify it?

options.why: Confused the multiplication sign between terms with a power of a power; a product adds the indices.
Division of powers of the same base subtracts the indices, it does not multiply them.
Addition is collecting like terms, giving $2t^{6}$; no index law applies.

questions.solution_text:
$\left(t^{6}\right)^{2}$
A power raised to a power multiplies the indices.
$=t^{12}$

options.why: Added the bracket's indices ($4+3$) instead of multiplying them, then subtracted $5$.
Simplified the bracket correctly but added $5$ instead of subtracting it.
Multiplied by the denominator's index instead of subtracting it.
Added the two known indices ($15+6$) instead of subtracting to undo the addition.
Multiplied the two known indices, treating the product as a power of a power.
Divided the indices ($15\div6$) instead of subtracting them.

questions.question_text:
A student writes $v^{8}\div v^{2}=1^{6}$.
What is the correct simplification of $v^{8}\div v^{2}$?

options.why: Divided the indices as $8\div2=4$ instead of subtracting them as $8-2$.
Subtracted the indices correctly to get $6$ but then wrote it as a coefficient, reading an index as a multiplier.
Made both slips: divided the indices to get $4$ and then wrote that $4$ as a coefficient instead of an index.

questions.solution_text:
$v^{8}\div v^{2}$
The base stays the same and only the indices are subtracted.
$=v^{8-2}$
$=v^{6}$

questions.question_text: Write $d^{3x+5}\times d^{2x-1}$ as a single power.

options.why: Added the $x$ terms but subtracted the constants, treating $-1$ as $+1$ to be taken away.
Subtracted both indices instead of adding them, as if the terms were divided.
Subtracted the $x$ terms while adding the constants.
